extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, students and researchers of evolutionary biology and ornithology (readers of Darwin)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and signs used to infer sexual selection and courtship function in birds (voice, instrumental sounds, ornaments, dances, and constructed displays), with counterexamples and mechanistic notes. Useful for assessing whether a trait evolved by sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male song as a sexual charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Male vocalizations (song/notes) function to charm or attract the female during courtship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive evidence includes singing concentrated in the breeding-season, males singing more and better than females, females responding or being attracted to the male's song, and specialised vocal organs or behaviours associated with courtship. Counterexamples are noted (some females sing well; males sometimes sing in autumn), so seasonality and behavioural context should be checked. Examples: black-cock's 'spel' attracting females; wild turkey male answering the female's call with a distinct note; nightingales and many Insessores as songsters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singing independent of love (non-sexual functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bird singing can occur for reasons other than attracting mates (e.g., practice, pleasure, territoriality, emulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume all singing is sexual: evidence includes sterile hybrid canary singing at its own reflection and attacking it, males singing outside breeding-season (autumn), and birds singing apparently for pleasure (gliding, playing). When interpreting song, check for sterile/hybrid cases, mirror/self-directed singing, seasonality, and whether singing is paired with courtship context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as learned art (practice and imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Singing is partly an art improved by practice; songs may be learned from foster-parents or neighbours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: birds acquiring the song of foster parents or neighbouring caged birds; ability to teach tunes; improvement with practice. When inferring genetic vs cultural origins of song, evaluate rearing history, exposure to tutors, and variability explained by learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental sounds used in courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-vocal sounds produced by body parts (rattling quills, wing-scraping, drumming) serve as courtship signals or calls to females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sounds produced during courtship, absent or reduced outside breeding-season, and evoking female approach/response. Examples include peacocks and Birds of Paradise rattling quills, Tetrao umbellus 'drumming' by striking wings above back, grouse buzzing, woodpecker branch-striking, and hoopoe tapping its beak to a stone while swallowing air to produce sound. Distinguish these from purely defensive or foraging sounds by behavioural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized feather/feather-shaft modifications for sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain feathers are specially modified (shape, stiff shafts, excised webs) to produce characteristic sounds during display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct morphological evidence includes snipe outer-tail feathers with stiff sabre-shaped shafts producing the drumming 'bleating' when air flows past them; manakin secondary wing-feather exotic thickenings producing whip-like cracks; hummingbird primaries with dilated shafts producing shrill whistling. If feathers reproduce the sound when waved/manipulated, this supports adaptive modification. Check sexual dimorphism and breeding-season use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological sexual dimorphism tied to courtship (inflatable sacs, tracheal modifications, wattles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexually dimorphic anatomical structures (inflatable throat sacks, convoluted trachea, fleshy wattles, bare coloured skin) are associated with courtship sounds or visual displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tetrao cupido male bare orange-coloured neck-sacks inflated during display; male bustard throat-sack connected to an 'oak' sound; convoluted trachea in swans and some Anatidae linked to vocal differences. Evaluate presence, seasonality (inflation/colour change during breeding-season), and experimental/observational connections between structure and sound/display (e.g., pricking a sack reducing sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments concentrated on head and appendages
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural ornaments (plumes, crests, ear-tufts, wattles) are often centered on the head and adjacent regions and are deployed in courtship displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head ornaments may be erectile, inflatable, or vividly coloured and often change appearance during courtship (swell, intensify colour). Examples: Tragopan fleshy lappet and horn-like structures, hornbill scarlet wattle inflation, iris/beak coloration differences. When assessing ornament function, check display postures and whether females respond to head-region displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dichromatism and male-biased ornamentation as evidence of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked colour/ornament differences between sexes, especially brighter/more ornamented males, indicate sexual selection via female choice or male-male competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples: peacock vs peahen, many Birds of Paradise (males highly decorated; females obscure). Consider exceptions: some species have ornamented females or both sexes ornamented. Use presence, degree, and behavioral context of dimorphism to infer selection pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent ornament/feather modifications across taxa indicate common selectable pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous feather modifications (racket-shaped tips, denuded shafts, filamentous barbs) occurring in widely distinct groups suggest similar selection by aesthetic/functional female preferences and shared developmental tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: racket-shaped feathers in motmots, kingfishers, hummingbirds, some birds of paradise; denuded shaft tail-feathers in Paradisea apoda. Such convergence supports that certain modifications are readily produced and favored when females select for particular visual/sound effects. Consider developmental constraints and shared feather architecture when interpreting convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructed displays (bowers, dance-arenas) as strong evidence of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures built solely for courtship (bowers) or ritualized communal dances indicate sexual selection and active mate attraction strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features strengthening inference: the structure is built solely for courtship (not nest), decorated, used repeatedly in mating context, male as principal builder/performer, and evokes female approach. Example: Australian Bower-birds—male-built, decorated bowers used as 'halls of assemblage.' Also partridge-dances where ground is worn bare. Check whether both sexes use it for courtship and whether construction occurs under confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing modification-for-display from incidental use
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sounds/structures arise from existing parts used during excitement (inherited continued use) rather than by direct selection for display; caution is required before attributing adaptive sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: loud voices possibly resulting from 'inherited effects of the continued use of their vocal organs when excited by love, jealousy and rage'; males practising instincts for pleasure. To distinguish: look for morphological specialization, sexual dimorphism, correlation with mating success, and experimental evidence (e.g., structural alteration reducing signal). Absence of such lines of evidence weakens sexual-selection claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female preference as the causal mechanism for progressive exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Female choice for particular sounds/performances leads to gradual exaggeration and modification of male traits (feathers, muscles, sounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanistic inference supported if females preferentially mate with males exhibiting certain features and if successive small variations in trait (e.g., stronger/thicker feathers, louder notes) confer mating advantage. Darwin notes females may not notice tiny changes but respond to resultant superior sounds/performances. Examine behavioural mate-choice data, heritability of trait variants, and incremental morphological changes consistent with selection.
